source_text: οὐ προσέχοντες, ὅτι καὶ ἄγγελοι ἢ ὡς ἄνθρωποι ἡγιάσθησαν ὅπερ ἀληθές· κτιστοὶ γάρ, ἢ ἐλάττονες τῶν ἁγιασθέντων ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀνθρώπων καὶ μετεχόντων αὐτοῦ, καθεστᾶσιν. 6.7ν ὅτι μεθεκτὸν οὐσιωδῶς ἐστι· θεοῦ δὲ μόνον ἴδιον τοῦτο. ἡ κτίσις ἀμέθεκτός ἐστιν οὐσιωδῶς τῇ λογικῇ ψυχῇ, ὡς ἐνοικίζεσθαι αὐτήν· μόνου γὰρ θεοῦ ἴδιον τὸ οὕτως μετέχεσθαι. τὸ δ' ἅγιον πνεῦμα μεθεκτὸν οὐσιωδῶς ὑπάρχει ὡς ὁ πατὴρ καὶ ὁ υἱός, καθὰ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ εἴρηται λόγῳ. ἐπεὶ κἀνταῦθα, τοῦ πατρὸς ἅπαξ ἐνοικοῦντος τοῖς ἀξίοις, οἷον ἦν ἀναγκαῖον, εἰ μὴ δι' ἑνότητα τῆς θεϊκῆς φύσεως καὶ πλήρωσιν τὴν εἰς ἡμᾶς, συνεισβάλλειν καὶ συνειστρέχειν καὶ τὸν υἱὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα; ἀμέλει τοι οὐκ ἂν τίς ποτε ἕλοιτο φάναι πληθὺν οἱονείπως θεῶν κατοικεῖν ἐν ἡμῖν, ἀλλ' ἕνα κατά γε τὸ ἓν ἐν ἑνάδι θεότητος ὑπάρχειν τὰς τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις. 6.8ν ὅτι ἀγαθόν, αὐτοτίκτον τὰς ἐν τῇ κτίσει ἀγαθότητας καὶ ἀληθείας καὶ σοφίας καὶ ἀγάπας· καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ συνεπινοεῖται πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον. ἡ κτίσις ἔχει τὸ ἀγαθόν, μεταδούσης αὐτῇ τῆς ἐν μιᾷ θεότητι τριάδος, τῆς οὔσης αὐτὸ τἀγαθόν. καὶ ἔστι δεύτερον τὸ κατὰ μετοχὴν ἔχειν τι πρὸς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ μέτρον ἀγαθὸν τοῦ φύσει αὐτὸ τὸ πρῶτον καὶ ἀμέτρητον ἀγαθὸν ὑπάρχειν· καὶ οὐ συγκλώθεται οὐδὲ συντάττεται τῷ δημιουργῷ ἑνὶ καὶ πρωτουργῷ ἀγαθῷ· οὗ πάντα μὲν ἐφίεται, αὐτὸ δὲ οὐδενὸς, τὸ ἐν τῇ κτίσει εὑρισκόμενον ἀγαθόν, κἂν λέγηται ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ· «εὖ, δοῦλε ἀγαθέ,» καί· «ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ τῆς καρδίας προ φέρει τὸ ἀγαθόν». οὐ γάρ, ὡς εἰπεῖν, αὐτὸ τὸ ἐγκάρδιον καὶ κυρίως ὂν ἀγαθὸν λέγει, ἀλλὰ τὸ συνεζευγμένον καὶ πρέπον τῇ κτίσει. ἐκεῖνο γὰρ πληθύει τε καὶ τοῖς οἰκείοις ποιήμασιν φιλοτιμεῖται ἀγαθότητας, ὅπως ἂν ἐντεῦθεν ἕκαστα τῶν ὄντων σώζηται, καὶ ἐν ᾗ ἔλαχεν εἶναι τάξει διαμένῃ· καὶ αὐτό ἐστιν τὸ ἓν ἀγαθόν, αἴτιον πᾶσιν πάντων ἀγαθῶν· καὶ δι' αὐτὸ πράττεται τὸ κάτω ἀγαθόν· καὶ αὐτὸ σώζει πάντα, οἷς ἂν παρῇ, ὥσπερ τὸ κακὸν ἐκ προαιρέσεως ἡμῶν συμβαῖνον φθείρει. οὗ αἰσθόμενοι καὶ οἱ ἔξω φασίν; ὡς· οἱ κακοὶ τοῦτο μέγιστον ἔχουσιν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἀγαθόν· ἄλλους γὰρ ἐπιχειροῦντες κακοῦν, αὐτοὶ πρότεροι τῆς ἑαυτῶν ἀπολαύουσι μοχθηρίας. τὸ δὲ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ὡς προείρηται, ὑπάρχον αὐτὸ–ἀπροδεὲς–ἀγαθὸν καὶ ὅλον–ἀεὶ–πρὸς–πάντας–ὂν–ἀγαθὸν καὶ οὐ δεύτερον τοῦ ἑνὸς καὶ πρώτου ἀγαθοῦ, ἴσας τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ καὶ περὶ τούτου μαρτυρίας ἐδέξατο, ὡς ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ ἀπεδείχθη λόγῳ καὶ ὡς ὁ Ἔσδρας ὁ πρὸς τὴν θείαν παρρησιασάμενος ἀγαθότητα διὰ τὸ εἰδέναι, ὅτι κἂν πταίῃ τι, τὸ παθεῖν παρ' αὐτῆς οὐκ ἔνι, προεφήτευσεν· «καὶ τὸ πνεῦμά σου τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἔδωκας συνετίσαι αὐτούς.» καὶ Ματθαῖος δὲ καὶ Λουκᾶς αὐτὴν τὴν θεϊκὴν ἀγαθότητα τὸ πνεῦμα κατ' οὐσίαν εἶναι σημαίνοντες, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐπινοεῖσθαι «πᾶσαν δόσιν ἀγαθὴν καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον», ὁ μὲν ἔγραψεν· «πόσῳ μᾶλλον ὁ πατὴρ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ δώσει ἀγαθὰ τοῖς αἰτοῦσιν αὐτόν;» ὁ δέ· «πόσῳ μᾶλλον ὁ πατὴρ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ δώσει πνεῦμα ἅγιον τοῖς αἰτοῦσιν αὐτόν;» τρεπτῆς γάρ, ὅ ἐστιν κτιστῆς, οὐσίας ἴδιον τὸ ὑπ' ἄλλου ἀγαθύνεσθαι ἢ ἁγιάζεσθαι ἢ σοφίζεσθαι καὶ μὴ αὐτὴν ἀτρέπτως ὑπάρχειν ταῦτα. καὶ ὁ θεὸς δὲ ἐν Ἠσαίᾳ δεικνύς, ὡς οὔποτε τὰς πνευματικὰς αὐτοῦ εὐλογίας λήψεταί τις μὴ ἀνάπλεως πρότερον τῆς σοφίας καὶ συνέσεως τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος εὑρεθείς, ἔφη· «ἐπιθήσω τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐπὶ τὸ σπέρμα σου καὶ τὰς εὐλογίας μου ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα σου.» ᾧ ἑπόμενα ἔγραψε Παῦλος· «διὰ τοῦτο», φησίν, «καὶ ἡμεῖς, ἀφ' ἧς ἡμέρας ἠκούσαμεν, οὐ παυ όμεθα ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν προσευχόμενοι καὶ αἰτούμενοι, ἵνα πληρωθῆτε τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ συνέσει πνευματι κῇ περιπατοῦντες ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου.» δῆλον δέ, 61 ὅτι λέγει· τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος. συνεπινοεῖσθαι γὰρ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ἄνω ἀτελεύτητον βασιλείαν, ὡς μὴ ἀλλοτρίαν αὐτοῦ τυγχάνουσαν διὰ τὴν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὸν υἱὸν ἀλληλουχίαν. καὶ αὖθις διὰ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐπιστολῆς πιστοῦται, γράφων· «οὐ γάρ ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ βρῶσις καὶ πόσις, ἀλλὰ δικαιο σύνη καὶ εἰρήνη καὶ χαρὰ ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ.» οὐκ ἔλαθεν δ' οὐδὲ τοῦτο καὶ Πέτρον. ἀπολογούμενος γὰρ τοῖς αἰτιωμένοις τὴν συντυχίαν, ἣ ἐποιήσατο πρὸς Κορνήλιον, ἔφη· «εἰ οὖν τὴν ἴσην δωρεὰν δέδωκεν αὐτοῖς ὁ θεός, παρασχὼν τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα, ὡς καὶ ἡμῖν ἐν ἀρχῇ· ἐγὼ τίς ἤμην δυνατὸς κωλῦσαι τὸν θεόν;» καὶ πάλιν· «καὶ ὁ καρδιογνώστης θεὸς ἐμαρτύρησεν αὐτοῖς, δοὺς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, καθὼς καὶ ἡμῖν·
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: they assert that the angels were not sanctified and yet are holy,] not paying attention to the fact that angels too either were sanctified as men were, which is true, for they are created; or else they stand lower than the men who were sanctified by God and share in him. 6.7ν [Chapter title:] That it is shared in substantially; and this is proper to God alone. The creation cannot be shared in substantially by the rational soul, so as to make its dwelling in it; for to be shared in this way is proper to God alone. But the Holy Spirit is shared in substantially, as the Father and the Son are, as was said in the first book. Since here too, when the Father once dwells in the worthy, how was it necessary, unless because of the unity of the divine nature and the fullness that comes to us, for both the Son and the Holy Spirit to burst in together and run in together? Certainly no one would ever choose to say that a multitude of gods, as it were, dwells in us, but one, at least in that the three hypostases exist as one in a unity of Godhead. 6.8ν [Chapter title:] That it is good, itself giving birth to the goodnesses and truths and wisdoms and loves in the creation; and in it every good giving and every perfect gift is understood together. The creation has the good, because the Trinity in one Godhead, which is the Good itself, has given it a share. And to have some good by participation, according to one's own measure, is second to being by nature the first and unmeasured Good itself. And the good found in the creation is not spun together with, nor ranked with, the creating, one and first-working Good, which all things desire, but which itself desires nothing; even if it is said in the Gospel: 'Well done, good servant,' and: 'The good man out of the good treasure of the heart brings forth the good.' For it does not, so to speak, speak of the inmost good itself, which is good in the proper sense, but of the good that is yoked to the creation and fitting for it. For that Good both abounds and lavishes goodnesses on its own works, so that by this each of the things that are may be preserved and may remain in the rank in which it was allotted to be; and it is the one Good, cause to all of all goods; and through it the good below is done; and it preserves all things to which it is present, just as evil, which comes about from our choice, destroys. Perceiving this, even those outside say: the wicked have this greatest good in themselves; for while trying to harm others, they themselves are the first to reap the fruit of their own wickedness. But the Holy Spirit, as was said before, being the very good that lacks nothing and the good that is whole, always, toward all, and not second to the one and first Good, received also on this point testimonies equal to the Father and the Son, as was shown in the first book, and as Ezra, who spoke boldly toward the divine goodness because he knew that, even if one stumbles in something, it is not possible to suffer harm from it, prophesied: 'And you gave your good Spirit to give them understanding.' And Matthew and Luke, signifying that the Spirit is in substance the divine goodness itself, and that in him is understood 'every good giving and every perfect gift', the one wrote: 'How much more will the Father from heaven give good things to those who ask him?' and the other: 'How much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?' For it is proper to a changeable, that is, a created, substance to be made good or sanctified or made wise by another, and not itself to be these things unchangeably. And God too in Isaiah, showing that no one will ever receive his spiritual blessings who has not first been found full of the wisdom and understanding of the Holy Spirit, said: 'I will put my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children.' Following which Paul wrote: 'For this reason,' he says, 'we too, from the day we heard, do not cease praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will, in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, walking worthily of the Lord.' And it is clear [printed line number 61, page debris] that he means 'of the divine Spirit'. For [he means] that the endless kingdom above is understood together with the Spirit of God, as not being foreign to him because of his mutual bond with the Father and the Son. And again through the same epistle he confirms it, writing: 'For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.' Nor did this escape Peter either. For, making his defence to those who found fault with the meeting he had with Cornelius, he said: 'If then God gave them the equal gift, providing the Holy Spirit, as also to us at the beginning, who was I, able to hinder God?' and again: 'And God who knows the heart bore witness to them, giving the Holy Spirit, just as also to us; [the quotation continues in the next section].
pass_b_english: …not noticing that either the angels too were sanctified, as men were, which is true, since they are created; or else they stand lower than the men who have been sanctified by God and share in him.
That he is shared in by substance, which is proper to God alone.

No creature can be shared in by the rational soul in its very substance, so as to make its dwelling in the soul; to be shared in this way is proper to God alone. But the Holy Spirit is shared in by substance, as the Father and the Son are, as was said in the first book. Here too, once the Father dwells in the worthy, why would the Son and the Holy Spirit have to burst in and run in with him, if not because of the unity of the divine nature and the fullness that comes to us? Surely no one would ever choose to say that a crowd of gods, as it were, dwells in us. It is one God, since the three hypostases are one in a unity of Godhead.
That he is good, and himself gives birth to the goodness, truth, wisdom and love found in creation; and that every good giving and every perfect gift is understood to be in him.

Creation has the good because the Trinity in one Godhead, which is the Good itself, has given it a share. To have some good by participation, according to one’s own measure, ranks second to being by nature the first and unmeasured Good itself. The good found in creation is not woven together with the one creating and first-working Good, nor ranked with it. All things desire that Good; it desires nothing. This holds even though the Gospel says, “Well done, good servant” (Matthew 25:21), and, “The good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart” (Luke 6:45). For it is not speaking, so to say, of the inmost good, good in the proper sense, but of the good that is joined to creation and fitting for it.

That Good abounds, and lavishes goodness on its own works, so that by it each thing that exists may be preserved and remain in the rank it was allotted. It is the one Good, the cause of all good things for all. Through it the good here below is done. It preserves everything to which it is present, just as evil, which springs from our own choice, destroys. Even those outside the Church have seen this, and say: “The wicked have this greatest good in themselves: while they try to harm others, they are the first to reap the fruit of their own wickedness.”

But the Holy Spirit, as was said before, is the very Good that lacks nothing, the good that is whole, always and toward all, and not second to the one and first Good. On this point too he has received testimonies equal to those given the Father and the Son, as was shown in the first book. So Ezra, who spoke boldly to the divine goodness because he knew that, even if one stumbles, no harm can come from that goodness, prophesied: “And you gave your good Spirit to instruct them” (Nehemiah 9:20).

Matthew and Luke also show that the Spirit is in substance the divine goodness itself, and that “every good giving and every perfect gift” (James 1:17) is understood to be in him. The one wrote, “How much more will the Father from heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:11), and the other, “How much more will the Father from heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13). For it is proper to a changeable substance, that is, a created one, to be made good or sanctified or made wise by another, and not to be these things itself without change.

God too, in Isaiah, shows that no one will ever receive his spiritual blessings who has not first been found full of the wisdom and understanding of the Holy Spirit, when he says, “I will put my Spirit upon your seed and my blessings upon your children” (Isaiah 44:3). In keeping with this Paul wrote: “For this reason,” he says, “we also, from the day we heard, have not stopped praying for you and asking that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, walking worthily of the Lord” (Colossians 1:9-10). It is clear that by “spiritual” he means “of the divine Spirit.” He means that the endless kingdom above is understood together with the Spirit of God, and is not foreign to him, because of his close bond with the Father and the Son. And again, in the same epistle, he confirms it when he writes, “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

Nor did this escape Peter. Defending himself to those who found fault with his meeting with Cornelius, he said: “If then God gave them the same gift, granting the Holy Spirit, as he did to us at the beginning, who was I, that I could hinder God?” (Acts 11:17). And again: “And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as he did to us…” (Acts 15:8).

choices.issue: Garbled machine draft with reversed claims, chapter titles run into the text, missing references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u15): retranslated from the Greek. The old English made the opening dilemma about angels into 'angels or men were regarded as holy', ran the chapter titles 6.7 and 6.8 into the paragraphs ('That participation is not essentially participative'; 'creation itself self-produces the goodnesses'), said the Trinity 'is not the Good itself' where the Greek says it is, turned 'which all things desire, but it desires nothing' into 'of whom all things flow, but He Himself is nothing of it', read προαιρέσεως as 'preconception', 'the first Word' for the first book, and lost the Spirit's 'not second to the one and first Good'. References: (Matt 25:21) written out; Luke 6:45, Nehemiah 9:20, James 1:17, Matthew 7:11, Luke 11:13, Isaiah 44:3, Colossians 1:9-10, Romans 14:17, Acts 11:17 and Acts 15:8 added. The bracket [primordial good] removed.

choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence, continuing the Macedonian claim at the end of u15-open; only this section's words are translated.
The copy-text numbers only these chapter titles here; each becomes its own paragraph without the number.

choices.term: ἡ κτίσις ἀμέθεκτός ἐστιν οὐσιωδῶς τῇ λογικῇ ψυχῇ
choices.english: No creature can be shared in by the rational soul in its very substance
choices.why: ἡ κτίσις here means any created being; 'no creature' keeps the claim and reads aloud.

choices.english: the fullness that comes to us
choices.why: The indwelling Trinity fills the worthy; the Son and Spirit come in with the Father because the Godhead is one.

choices.term: αὐτοτίκτον τὰς ... ἀγαθότητας καὶ ἀληθείας καὶ σοφίας καὶ ἀγάπας
choices.english: himself gives birth to the goodness, truth, wisdom and love found in creation
choices.why: The Greek plurals ('goodnesses, truths') are the many created forms of each; English singular abstracts carry that without awkwardness.
Didymus plays on 'treasure of the heart': the Gospel's 'good' is not the good at the core of being, good in the strict sense.

The standard patristic term for pagan writers; 'the Church' is added so the phrase is understood and adds no claim. The saying echoes a Greek proverb (compare Hesiod, Works and Days 265); not Scripture.

choices.english: the very Good that lacks nothing, the good that is whole, always and toward all
choices.why: The edition hyphenates these as compound titles; English keeps them as piled phrases.
Nehemiah 9:20 stands in the Greek Bible's 2 Esdras, where the prayer is introduced 'And Ezra said' (LXX Nehemiah 9:6); Didymus' attribution is kept.

choices.term: δῆλον δέ, 61 ὅτι λέγει· τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος
choices.english: It is clear that by “spiritual” he means “of the divine Spirit.”
choices.why: 61 is a printed line number, page debris, skipped. 'by “spiritual”' is added to show which word of the quotation is being explained; it adds no claim.
Didymus says 'the same epistle' after quoting Colossians, but the words are Romans 14:17. His wording is kept and the verse quoted is cited; recorded in problems.

choices.english: “If then God gave them the same gift … as he did to us at the beginning, who was I, that I could hinder God?”
choices.why: The quotation is Acts 11:17 with 'at the beginning' drawn from Acts 11:15; cited to 11:17, the verse it follows.

choices.english: just as he did to us…
choices.why: The quotation of Acts 15:8-9 runs on into the next section; the English ends with an ellipsis inside the quotation.
